main.title: Resident Evil Gaiden
main.subtitle: M4 · Game Boy Color
main.summary: Resident Evil Gaiden is M4's Game Boy Color adventure about Barry Burton searching for Leon Kennedy aboard a passenger ship struck by a viral outbreak. Corridors and rooms are explored from above, with weapons, keys and supplies supporting the search through the vessel. The smaller screen gives the ship a different form from the series' fixed-camera console spaces. An approaching zombie still creates an immediate problem, but entering combat changes the display and asks the player to handle the threat through timing rather than ordinary movement around the room.

cards.heading: An outbreak aboard the Starlight
cards.text: Resident Evil Gaiden is M4's Game Boy Color adventure about Barry Burton searching for Leon Kennedy aboard a passenger ship struck by a viral outbreak. Corridors and rooms are explored from above, with weapons, keys and supplies supporting the search through the vessel. The smaller screen gives the ship a different form from the series' fixed-camera console spaces. An approaching zombie still creates an immediate problem, but entering combat changes the display and asks the player to handle the threat through timing rather than ordinary movement around the room.

cards.heading: Stop the marker over the target
cards.text: Combat switches to a first-person arrangement with a marker moving across a horizontal bar. Pressing the action button when it aligns with the enemy determines the attack's result. The encounter separates aiming from the exploration controls, turning each shot into a brief timing challenge. Ammunition and healing items remain useful discoveries aboard the ship. The player moves between carefully checking the map and reacting to the next creature, with the cost of a failed attempt carrying back into the resources available for the continuing search.

cards.heading: A different portable interpretation of the series
cards.text: Barry and Leon encounter Lucia, a girl with an unusual connection to the weapon being carried aboard the Starlight. Their investigation gives the changing decks and corridors a continuing mystery beyond the immediate outbreak. Published first in Europe in 2001, Gaiden takes the series' characters and equipment into a substantially different structure. Its uneven reception reflected that change, but it remains a distinctive adaptation of survival horror to the handheld: exploration preserves the careful management of supplies, while fighting compresses the dangerous instant of a shot into a readable moving target.

main.title: Mega Man Battle Network 2
main.summary: Mega Man Battle Network 2 is a 2001 tactical role-playing game developed by Capcom for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) handheld game console.

cards.text: Mega Man Battle Network 2 is a 2001 tactical role-playing game developed by Capcom for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) handheld game console. It is the second game in the Mega Man Battle Network series, and a sequel to the first game; it follows Lan Hikari and his NetNavi, MegaMan.EXE, as they attempt to take down the new NetCrime syndicate Gospel.

Mega Man Battle Network 2 received generally positive reviews, with many praising it for improving upon the gameplay of the first entry; it has been re-released multiple times, including via the Wii U Virtual Console in 2014, and as part of the Mega Man Battle Network Legacy Collection compilation in 2023. It was followed up by Mega Man Battle Network 3 in 2002.

main.title: Ikaruga
main.summary: Ikaruga (literally 'Japanese grosbeak') is a bullet hell game developed by Treasure.

cards.heading: Black and white change what a bullet means
cards.text: Ikaruga (literally 'Japanese grosbeak') is a bullet hell game developed by Treasure. It is the spiritual sequel to Radiant Silvergun (1998) and was originally released in Japanese arcades in December 2001. The story follows a rebel pilot named Shinra as he battles an enemy nation using a specially designed fighter called the Ikaruga which can flip between two polarities, black and white. This polarity mechanism is the game's key feature and the foundation for its stage and enemy design. All enemies and bullets in the game are either black or white. Bullets which are the same color as the player are absorbed while the others will kill the player. The game features both single-player and cooperative modes.

cards.heading: A prototype refines the rhythm of absorption
cards.text: Development on Ikaruga began during director Hiroshi Iuchi's off-hours while Treasure was busy developing Sin and Punishment (2000). Titled "Project RS2", the game began as a sequel to Radiant Silvergun, and borrows many elements from it as well as the polarity mechanism from Treasure's Silhouette Mirage (1997). During the game's prototype stages, the player's ammo was limited. The bullet absorption mechanism was used as a means to refill ammo. However, this was found to be weak as it created too many breaks in the action so it was later added as an additional mode in home ports. In tradition with Treasure's game design philosophy, Ikaruga was intentionally crafted to challenge the conventions of standard game design and develop a new type of shooting game. All together, five Treasure staff worked on Ikaruga, as well as three support staff from G.rev.

cards.heading: A demanding shooter finds its audience
cards.text: Upon its initial release in Japanese arcades, reception was mixed. Treasure staff explained this was due to players expecting a more standard shooter offering but instead being greeted with a different game system that featured more puzzle-like elements rather than the twitch gameplay of bullet-dodging. In 2002, Ikaruga was ported to the Dreamcast in Japan and began to grow a cult following from import gamers worldwide. It was later released in the West in 2003 on the GameCube, receiving positive reviews. Critics praised the graphics as well as the art and sound design. Some criticism was directed towards its difficulty. Most critics felt the unique game design choices were innovative, while some believed they stifled many of the classic shooter elements. Ikaruga was later ported to the Xbox 360, Windows, Nintendo Switch, and PlayStation 4. In retrospect, Ikaruga is regarded by critics as one of the best games ever made, especially in the shoot 'em up genre, and one of Treasure's greatest works.

main.title: Sonic Advance
main.summary: Sonic Advance is a 2001 platform game developed by Sonic Team and Dimps and published by Sega for the Game Boy Advance.

cards.text: Sonic Advance is a 2001 platform game developed by Sonic Team and Dimps and published by Sega for the Game Boy Advance. It was one of the first Sonic the Hedgehog games to be released on a Nintendo console along with Sonic Adventure 2: Battle on the GameCube, and was produced in commemoration of the series' tenth anniversary. The story follows Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, and Amy as they journey to stop Doctor Eggman from taking over the world. Controlling a character, players are tasked with completing each level, defeating Eggman and his robot army, and collecting the seven Chaos Emeralds.

Development began after Sega shifted its focus to third-party software development, due to the poor performance of the Dreamcast console. Sega recruited Dimps to lead development, making the game the first in the franchise developed by the studio. While Sonic Advance follows a similar style of gameplay to the Sega Genesis Sonic games, certain concepts and designs were reused from newer games such as Sonic Adventure (1998). The game was ported to Nokia's N-Gage in 2003 as SonicN, with ports to J2ME devices by Gameloft and Android by Sega releasing in 2011. The GBA version was re-released on the Wii U's Virtual Console in Japan.

Sonic Advance received positive reviews for its graphics, character animations, and faithfulness to the original Genesis games, but also received criticism for its short length and special stages. It was a commercial success, selling 1.21 million copies in the United States and is among the GBA's bestselling games. The game was followed by two sequels also on the Game Boy Advance; Sonic Advance 2 (2002) and Sonic Advance 3 (2004).

main.title: Blood Wake
main.subtitle: Gunboats carry the action across a changing sea
main.summary: Blood Wake is Stormfront Studios' Xbox naval combat game, released in North America on 28 December 2001. Its fictional, Asian-influenced setting provides a campaign of raids, attacks, escorts and defensive missions fought entirely from small armed vessels. The player moves across the water while aiming the boat's weapons and responding to threats around the route. Sea and sky conditions help distinguish locations without taking the action onto land. The boat becomes both the means of travelling through the environment and the fighting platform that must survive long enough to complete the assignment.

cards.heading: Gunboats carry the action across a changing sea
cards.text: Blood Wake is Stormfront Studios' Xbox naval combat game, released in North America on 28 December 2001. Its fictional, Asian-influenced setting provides a campaign of raids, attacks, escorts and defensive missions fought entirely from small armed vessels. The player moves across the water while aiming the boat's weapons and responding to threats around the route. Sea and sky conditions help distinguish locations without taking the action onto land. The boat becomes both the means of travelling through the environment and the fighting platform that must survive long enough to complete the assignment.

cards.heading: Choose a line through the water and the fire
cards.text: Playable vessels range from small craft to more heavily armed boats, with primary guns supplemented by weapons such as torpedoes, rockets and mines. The available configuration changes how close a target should be approached and which direction is safest after an attack. Escort work also introduces something that needs to remain alive besides the player's own vessel. A successful run therefore involves movement as much as accurate firing. The player needs to maintain a useful angle, avoid surrounding fire and recognise when pressing an attack would leave the mission's more vulnerable objective exposed.

cards.heading: An early Xbox game finds variety on the water
cards.text: The campaign contains twenty-eight missions, while local multiplayer supports up to four players and unlocks additional options through story progress. Hidden boats and modes include a deliberately extravagant form of football played by armed vessels with a giant ball. Blood Wake received mixed reviews but sold enough to join the Xbox Platinum Hits range. Its unusual setting helped distinguish the console's early catalogue. Instead of treating the sea as an interval between land-based battles, it builds the entire action game around the speed, turning and weapon positions of the craft travelling across it.

main.title: Akira Yamaoka: a sound without warning
main.summary: Fear crosses music and sound design.

cards.heading: Choose a texture for a world
cards.text: Yamaoka described industrial sound as a deliberate way to distinguish Silent Hill. In a 2002 interview, he connected its cold, rusty character to the game's theme, through texture as well as melody. He also said he did not habitually listen to industrial music himself. His choice served the setting rather than following his usual listening habits. His explanation concerns choosing a material for a particular world, with an intended feeling that goes beyond personal listening habits.

cards.heading: Sound needs its surroundings
cards.text: He nevertheless insisted that sound could not carry the experience alone. Graphics, scenario and play had to support it, or its emotional force would weaken. The same interview describes trusting the main staff's shared understanding rather than needing to inspect every scene before composing. That shared understanding linked the music to the rest of production. Listening to the music separately can reveal its shape, but the composer himself placed its in-game effect inside an agreement among several parts of production.

cards.heading: Hear evidence before its cause
cards.text: In 2014, Yamaoka contrasted predictable accompaniment with atmospheric sound and noise used around an enemy's appearance. He wanted a sound to suggest something before a clear visual explanation arrived. The proposal concerns withheld information and musical style. A player hears evidence without necessarily seeing its cause. His description makes anticipation part of the composer's task, alongside choosing the textures and rhythms that a player hears. The boundary between a cue and an effect becomes useful precisely because the player cannot always classify what is heard.

cards.heading: A singer changes the possibility
cards.text: A singing voice introduced other decisions. Yamaoka recalled seeking vocals for Silent Hill 3, hearing audition material and eventually choosing Mary Elizabeth McGlynn, who had been working as an ADR director around the auditions. He valued the emotions her voice could convey. This recollection gives the performer a place within the sound's identity. A vocal track was not an instrumental composition with an interchangeable human sound added afterwards: finding a particular collaborator became part of deciding what the song could express within the game.

main.title: Gunvalkyrie
main.summary: Boost chains, weapon weight and mission scores turn an airborne fight into a route to learn and improve.

cards.heading: Gunvalkyrie
cards.text: Gunvalkyrie is Smilebit's third-person shooter for the original Xbox, published by Sega in 2002. Kelly and Saburouta investigate a colony overrun by insect-like creatures in an alternative history of space travel and British imperial technology. Their armoured suits turn each mission into a fight conducted between the ground and the air.

cards.heading: Staying above the swarm
cards.text: A boost carries Kelly past a swarm, but the next change of direction matters just as much as the first. Linking forward, sideways and backward boosts while enemies are nearby builds a combo and can strengthen her weapon. Landing, hovering or taking a hit breaks that sequence. Holding a useful height therefore becomes a skill of its own: keep the insects in view, find the next clear direction and change course before the attack reaches you.

cards.heading: A weapon changes the flight
cards.text: Kelly's Heat Blaster lets her keep moving while she locks onto targets. Her heavier Drive Gun changes that relationship: firing on the ground holds her still, while firing in the air puts her into a hover and cancels the boost combo. Saburouta offers greater initial firepower with less mobility and a narrower attack range. Choosing a character and weapon changes the space needed for an attack, and the time spent exposed while making it.

cards.heading: The next attempt
cards.text: The mission briefing describes the terrain, enemies and objective before deployment. Afterwards, the results screen rewards speed, defeated enemies and kills made with combo-enhanced shots, while damage lowers the clear bonus. Part of that score becomes GVP to spend on weapons and armour. A successful run can therefore fund the equipment for a better one; learning where a swarm appears or where a hidden Halley Core lies has a lasting use beyond reaching the exit.

main.title: RalliSport Challenge
main.subtitle: Four disciplines across loose ground and ice
main.summary: RalliSport Challenge brought Digital Illusions CE's racing experience to Xbox in 2002, followed by a Windows version later that year. Microsoft published a game built around four forms of off-road competition: rally, hill climb, rallycross and ice racing. Switching disciplines changes both the shape of a course and the kind of contest taking place on it, from a timed run through open country to several cars sharing a frozen circuit.

cards.heading: Off the road
cards.text: RalliSport Challenge brought Digital Illusions CE's racing experience to Xbox in 2002, followed by a Windows version later that year. Microsoft published a game built around four forms of off-road competition: rally, hill climb, rallycross and ice racing. Switching disciplines changes both the shape of a course and the kind of contest taking place on it, from a timed run through open country to several cars sharing a frozen circuit.

cards.heading: A clock or a field of rivals
cards.text: The discipline selection makes these differences visible before a race begins. Rally and hill climb ask for a fast run along a route, with each mistake carried into the final time. Rallycross and ice racing put other cars into the same corners. A clear racing line can disappear when another driver occupies it. The challenge moves between remembering the road ahead and making room for a rival who may be sliding across the intended exit.

cards.heading: Reading the surface
cards.text: On an ice circuit, a small steering input can develop into a long slide. The player has to prepare for a bend before reaching it, leaving enough space for the car to settle on the way out. Dirt and gravel stages change the visual rhythm: spectators, trees and roadside structures pass close to the route. The cars' movement, thrown-up particles and distinct engine sounds make these different surfaces part of the driving experience.

cards.heading: A career across disciplines
cards.text: Career events unlock further cars and tracks as results improve. The variety gives progress a practical purpose: a new event may require a different approach to braking, overtaking or carrying speed. Returning to a familiar car does not guarantee the same response from every course. The Windows edition extended the competition to network play, while bringing the original Xbox game's combination of country stages and shared circuits to another audience.

main.title: Taz: Wanted
main.subtitle: A whirlwind with a price on its head
main.summary: Escaping the zoo is only the beginning when destruction is your most useful skill.

cards.heading: Sam’s unwanted attraction
cards.text: Developed by Blitz Games and published by Infogrames, Taz: Wanted appeared in 2002 for PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube and Windows. Yosemite Sam captures Taz and plans to turn his home into a theme park. Escape makes Taz a fugitive, with wanted posters and pursuers turning each new location into another attempt to keep moving. The deliberately exaggerated environments give the Tasmanian Devil room to become a destructive force.

cards.heading: Spin, swallow, improvise
cards.text: Spinning, bouncing, eating and spitting provide ways to break obstacles and deal with enemies. Disguises change how Taz approaches particular situations, while destroying wanted posters gives his rampage a clear objective. Each power or costume offers a different way through the obstacles. Nimrod Productions receives the game’s music credit.

main.title: Gran Turismo Concept 2001 Tokyo
main.subtitle: From motor-show stand to racetrack
main.summary: Polyphony Digital turns a selection from the Tokyo Motor Show into a concentrated driving game.

cards.heading: From motor-show stand to racetrack
cards.text: Gran Turismo Concept 2001 Tokyo brings prototypes from the Tokyo Motor Show onto PlayStation 2 racetracks. Polyphony Digital selects fewer cars and courses than Gran Turismo 3, creating a shorter game focused on trying the vehicles. Concepts, hybrids and new sports cars capture the manufacturers' ideas at the beginning of the 2000s.

cards.heading: Trying the prototypes
cards.text: The selection includes the Nissan GT-R Concept, Toyota pod and Honda Dualnote, alongside production sports cars and imagined racing versions. PlayStation 2 stations at the 2001 Tokyo show let visitors try the game. Cars displayed on stands could also be experienced through acceleration, steering and a route around a circuit.

cards.heading: A concentrated Gran Turismo
cards.text: The reduced selection was intended partly to make the game friendlier to beginners. Its structure resembles an expanded arcade mode, giving quick access to the cars in place of the main series' long career and economic progression. That concentrated format keeps attention on the chosen vehicles and the immediate pleasure of driving them.

cards.heading: The future as manufacturers imagined it
cards.text: Some concept cars anticipated ideas that reached production, while others remained styling exercises or became imagined racing versions in the game. The selection covers future sports cars, four-wheel-drive designs and hybrids. Preserving them together records the shapes and technical expectations manufacturers were presenting at that moment.
